\x1b[38;5;246m\x1b[48;5;237m❯ \x1b[38;5;231mWrite a 300-word story about a lighthouse. Plain text, no tools.\x1b[39m
\x1b[49m
\x1b[38;5;231m⏺\x1b[39m The lighthouse on Carrick Point had not dimmed in ninety-one years, and Marta intended to keep it that way.

  She inherited the post from her uncle, who inherited it from a woman named Ruth Ansel, whose name was painted in faded gold above the door of the keeper's
  cottage. Marta had read the logbooks. Every night for almost a century, someone had written the same few words: \x1b[3mLamp lit. Weather fair. Nothing seen.\x1b[0m

  The storm arrived on a Tuesday in October. The wind came off the water like a shoulder against a door, and the sea climbed the rocks until spray hit the
  lantern glass. Marta climbed the iron stairs with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, her boots slipping on the wet treads. At the top, the lamp hummed and
  flickered. A cracked wick, or a failing generator. She did not know which. She only knew the light had to stay on.

  She worked until her fingers bled. Somewhere past midnight, the flame steadied.

  When dawn came gray and thin, she climbed the stairs again and looked out. The water was calming. A fishing boat, small and battered, was limping toward the
  harbor, its running lights blinking weakly. It was the first ship she had seen in three days.

  She sat down on the cold floor beneath the lens and opened the logbook. Her pen hovered over the page, then began to move.

  \x1b[3mLamp lit. Weather rough. One boat seen, safe home.\x1b[0m

  She closed the book and, for the first time since arriving, smiled.
